summary: The build can start: the machine has Python, Node, Docker, the documentdb MCP server, and the DocumentDB agent skills the sample needs. Key facts that a coding agent might have recalled from memory are incorrect or ambiguous (mostly because the product has a new vCore / mongoClusters surface that differs from the older Cosmos DB / databaseAccounts model). Missing command-line tools (mongosh) and a small set of unanswered implementation details (SWIFT sample payloads and precise Python package pins) will require minor workarounds but do not block the sample.
summary_points: Core build tools present: python (3.13), Node (24.x), docker, az signed-in, the documentdb MCP server and many documentdb-* skills are installed — the app code can be written and verified against the live cluster.

Several cold answers were incorrect because the managed Mongo offering now uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (vCore) and az documentdb mongocluster commands rather than Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb; using the wrong resource type or CLI would break any IaC or CLI steps.

Authentication, vector and full-text search, change-streams, and local development behavior differ from older Cosmos DB (RU) accounts — the authoritative docs show Microsoft Entra ID auth, DiskANN/HNSW/IVF vector indexes, integrated $search full-text and hybrid BM25+vector, and a local DocumentDB docker gateway (port 10260).
Missing developer tooling: mongosh isn't on PATH (inventory). Workarounds exist (use the documentdb MCP tools and driver-based checks), but adding mongosh will make manual verification easier.
Information gaps: the sample needs SWIFT MT103/MT202 canonical sample messages and a mapping of fields → document schema; no skill or docs in the environment provide SWIFT field schemas.
Verdict=ready_with_gaps: build proceeds, but follow the corrected facts and fill the two small information/tool gaps noted below.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a Cosmos/DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current managed Mongo (vCore) cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts). Use the mongoClusters resource under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider to deploy vCore clusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-arm-template)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) resource model historically hosted the 'Cosmos' family, and many docs and samples still reference Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB. The new vCore-managed Mongo service uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters) under the same provider.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (connect docs referencing databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and az cosmosdb CLI commands or ARM/Bicep resource types for cluster creation / IAM, IaC would target the wrong control-plane object and attempts to create or manage a vCore cluster would fail or provision the wrong service.
improvements: Add a prominent sentence to the Azure DocumentDB quickstarts and the agent kit landing page clarifying that vCore Mongo clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and az documentdb mongocluster commands (link to the mongoClusters template doc).
Add a deprecation/rename note to older pages that still use databaseAccounts when the correct resource type for vCore clusters is mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb (e.g. az cosmosdb create...). This is part of the main Azure CLI distribution (not a separate extension).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct current CLI group for vCore-managed Mongo clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g. az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list-connection-strings). These commands are available in the az CLI module that exposes documentdb mongocluster commands (the Azure CLI will prompt to install extensions for first-use in some setups).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB docs and many samples use az cosmosdb for Cosmos DB accounts; the new vCore/managed-Mongo offering uses its own az documentdb mongocluster command group. Shared provider namespace and historical product names caused the conflation.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would operate on different resource types (Cosmos DB databaseAccounts) and not create or manage the vCore mongoClusters the sample expects; CLI-based IaC or scripts would fail or produce the wrong resources.
improvements: Document the az documentdb mongocluster command group prominently in the agent kit's deployment guidance and add an explicit 'Do not use az cosmosdb for vCore mongoClusters' note on older quickstarts.
Ensure the DocumentDB MCP or agent skill provides a single section that maps old CLI groups (az cosmosdb) → new az documentdb commands for vCore scenarios.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Mongo clusters the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM) and Terraform/AzAPI usage targets that resource (examples and Azure Verified Modules are published). The azurerm_cosmosdb_account / Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts resource is the older Cosmos DB account model (RU-based) and not the vCore mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-arm-template)
Azure Verified Modules: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) (bicep/avm)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historic Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) naming and the older azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform resource correspond to the RU-based Cosmos model; the new vCore mongoClusters resource is distinct though it lives under the same provider namespace.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder authored Bicep/Terraform using databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account the templates would not deploy the vCore mongoCluster resources required by the sample, producing a mismatch between IaC and the cluster the run-environment requires.
improvements: Add a 'resource type decision' note to the documentdb-azure-deployment skill that explicitly maps common IaC resources to the correct resource type (mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts) and shows a minimal Bicep example for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. TLS port is 10255; schemes mongodb or mongodb+srv are used by drivers but standard Cosmos Mongo URIs commonly use mongodb:// with ssl=true and retryWrites=false and replicaSet=globaldb.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the current DocumentDB vCore clusters the common form is mongodb+srv://<client-or-user>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (or mongodb+srv with MONGODB-OIDC/OIDC properties for Microsoft Entra auth). The host name suffix and port differ from older Cosmos RU endpoints; connection strings and SRV forms are provided by az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings / portal. Local DocumentDB gateway uses port 10260 in the development loop.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (examples showing mongodb+srv and TLS)
Development loop (DocumentDB local Docker gateway port 10260 connection string example)
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (API/CLI)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Different managed Mongo offerings (classic Cosmos DB for Mongo API vs vCore mongoClusters) use different host suffixes (documents.azure.com vs mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and ports (older Cosmos examples used 10255; local gateway uses 10260). Old examples and older Cosmos docs still describe the 10255/documents.azure.com pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB (classic Cosmos Mongo docs showing port 10255 example)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or the wrong auth mechanism in code can cause connection failures or insecure connections (if TLS options are omitted). Using SRV vs non-SRV forms incorrectly also affects driver behavior.
improvements: Ensure the quickstart and sample README explicitly show the cluster-provided connection string format (SRV vs non-SRV) and call out the local Docker gateway port 10260 example in the development loop doc.
Add a sample Python snippet in the documentdb-driver skill that shows reading DOCUMENTDB_URI and passing tls=True/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates in dev vs production.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is RU/s (provisioned throughput) or autoscale RU/s; serverless is available in some regions. There is also a newer vCore/dedicated compute offering for MongoDB-compatible workloads in some SKUs, but the classic Cosmos model is RU-based billing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore-managed Mongo offering) is billed by compute tier (vCores/tiers such as M30, M40) and storage; it is not RU/s based. The RU-based Cosmos DB model is a different offering (Cosmos RU-based accounts). The vCore model bills per-node tier + storage and supports M30 etc as listed in the product pricing docs.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB offered RU/s billing and some docs still present that model for Cosmos accounts; the new DocumentDB vCore offering uses compute-tier billing. The word 'DocumentDB' and overlap in naming causes confusion.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (classic RU/Autoscale docs referencing RU-based billing)

confusions.build_risk: If a builder plans on using RU-based commands or expects RU autoscale semantics (for example, setting throughput via RU APIs), those operations won't apply to the vCore mongoClusters; provisioning and scaling code will be wrong.
improvements: Add a short 'billing model' callout on the top of the mongoClusters quickstart page explaining 'vCore (tiered) billing' vs 'Cosmos RU-based' and link to the pricing page.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you use database user credentials (username/password). Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is not generally available for the MongoDB wire-protocol endpoint — drivers authenticate with the Mongo credentials (username/password / SCRAM mechanisms).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters support both Native (username/password SCRAM) auth and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication. Entra ID support must be enabled on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes including MicrosoftEntraID), and drivers or tools can connect using MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC-style connection strings (examples in docs include mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties specifying ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE...).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (how-to and connection-string examples)
Enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication (Bicep/CLI examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts historically lacked full Entra/AAD OIDC flow for Mongo; the vCore mongoClusters added explicit Microsoft Entra ID support and OIDC connection-string patterns, and the CLI has options to enable it.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB docs that focus on primary key / username/password connection strings

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes Entra ID is unsupported they may try to use static DB admin/passwords for long-lived credentials rather than enabling role-based identity flows for managed identities; conversely, if they attempt to use MONGODB-OIDC without enabling Entra on the cluster the connection will fail.
improvements: Add a short 'Enable Entra ID' checklist to the documentdb-mcp-setup or documentdb-azure-deployment skills showing how to flip authConfig.allowedModes and register managed identities, with a minimal connector example using the OIDC connection string.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo, motor for async Python) or ODMs built on them (Beanie on motor). There is no separate Mongo-protocol-specific DocumentDB runtime SDK — you should use the official MongoDB driver for your language when targeting the Mongo API of Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use the standard MongoDB drivers (Motor for async Python) and Beanie (ODM) on top of Motor/pydantic for async Python. DocumentDB (vCore) exposes the MongoDB wire protocol so standard drivers are appropriate.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (drivers guidance)

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector index types available: HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. You create a vector index using the MongoDB createIndex command with a vector index spec on the field. Example pseudo-command: db.messages.createIndex( { embedding: "vector" }, { name: "emb_idx", algorithm: "hnsw", similarity: "cosine", dimensions: 1536, m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } ).
confusions.grounded_answer: Supported vector index kinds include vector-hnsw (HNSW), vector-ivf (IVF/IVFFLAT), and vector-diskann (DiskANN). The DocumentDB API uses a createIndexes-style payload with a specialized vector index options block (cosmosSearchOptions) rather than the generic createIndex vector: "vector" syntax. Example (schema fragment) uses key path + cosmosSearchOptions.kind = 'vector-hnsw' and parameters like dimensions, m, efConstruction (HNSW) or numLists (IVF) or DiskANN-specific params.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds & creation examples)
Vector store details (DiskANN/IVF/HNSW examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic MongoDB vector syntax (which some vector-enabled DBs adopt) rather than DocumentDB's documented createIndexes payload with cosmosSearchOptions and specific 'kind' strings. The index types (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) are correct, but the creation syntax differs.

confusion_sources.title: Generic createIndex vector syntax in some vector DBs (not authoritative for DocumentDB)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder copies the generic createIndex example, index creation API calls will fail or be ignored on the cluster; vector queries won't use the intended index.
improvements: Add a minimal Python or JS example to the documentdb-vector-search skill that shows the exact createIndexes payload and the key/cosmosSearchOptions shape for each 'kind'.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API does not expose an Atlas-style Lucene index. For full-text you typically integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or use app-side text processing. Hybrid is done by combining vector query + text match in app.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides integrated full-text search (BM25) via search indexes created with createSearchIndexes and queries via the $search aggregation stage. Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) is supported (BM25 + cosmosSearch vector) and can be combined in pipelines (the docs show a hybrid approach and RRF fusion guidance). You do not need a separate Azure Cognitive Search for many full-text or hybrid scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes, $search, BM25, hybrid guidance)
Full-text search + vector hybrid (what's available today)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts had more limited built-in full-text search features; many builders historically integrated Azure Cognitive Search. DocumentDB now includes an integrated search index and the $search operator, but older guidance and external blog posts still recommend external search.

confusion_sources.title: Guidance to integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (older approach or for advanced cases)

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes there is no integrated $search/full-text index they may architect extra infrastructure (Azure Cognitive Search) and ETL for search unnecessarily, increasing complexity and cost.
improvements: Update the documentdb-full-text-search skill with a short 'when to use integrated $search vs Azure Cognitive Search' decision table and add a quick Python example for createSearchIndexes + $search.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB-compatible API advertises support for specific MongoDB wire versions (newer accounts support newer versions; my target cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 compatibility). However, not every MongoDB feature is implemented: transactions limited to partition, some server-side features/commands may not be available.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0 and provides broad operator compatibility (99.03% of operators). Some server/admin commands and a small set of features differ due to the managed platform; the compatibility docs list supported/unsupported operators and server commands. Multi-shard operational admin commands are managed by the platform, and a compatibility check is recommended before migrating.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (wire protocol versions 5.0-8.0 described)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility summary including supported wire protocol versions)

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator; run a real MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) on 27017 and point your app at it. For testing against actual Cosmos behavior you must use a live Cosmos account.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a DocumentDB local Docker gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and guidance for a local development loop. The local gateway listens on port 10260 by default (gateway endpoint and example connection string provided in docs). Use that container for dev parity. For full feature parity you may still need a live cluster, but the local gateway exists and is documented.

grounding_links.title: Development loop (DocumentDB local Docker gateway and port 10260)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB (local Docker instructions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Some builders assume no local emulator because older Cosmos DB Mongo API lacked a promoted, supported local gateway image; DocumentDB now provides an OSS-based local gateway image and instructions.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no local gateway exists they may omit local-development scaffolding or write tests only for a remote cluster, slowing local iteration.
improvements: Add a 'local dev' quick snippet to documentdb-local-deployment skill showing the exact docker pull/run example and connection string format (port 10260).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change Streams support depends on the account's MongoDB API version; newer Mongo-compatible accounts support change streams but older/legacy accounts may not. If supported, you can use the standard driver change stream APIs. Some accounts may require the 'changeStream' capability or a specific server version to be enabled.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported by Azure DocumentDB. For multi-shard clusters or some scenarios the feature may be gated or require enabling a preview feature; the docs show guidance and where to enable change-stream-related features and mention a gated preview for multi-shard change streams in some releases. Builders should verify the cluster's features and enable the preview if needed.

grounding_links.title: Migrate and change-streams guidance (change streams gating/preview notes)
Tutorial notes referencing Model.watch() -> uses change streams and enabling change stream preview for multishard

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is cautious but imprecise: change streams are supported today but some advanced scenarios (multishard change stream gating/preview) require explicit enabling or may be in preview, so 'depends' is too vague without the docs that show how to enable it.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are always enabled they may write code that fails when run against a cluster that lacks the specific preview feature or required configuration.
improvements: Add a note to the documentdb-mcp-setup skill describing how to verify and enable change-stream features on the target cluster (portal/az resource patch/Bicep snippet).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' which provides data-plane inspection and tools for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general Azure MCP server covers many resource-plane operations, but the documentdb MCP server provides Mongo/Cosmos-specific collection/index inspection and query plan tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: There is a dedicated documentdb MCP server (data-plane) that provides document/collection/index/aggregation/explain tools; the azure MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but is not a substitute for the documentdb data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory entry)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Originally Microsoft marketed a service called Azure DocumentDB (the JSON/document DB) which later became part of Azure Cosmos DB as the SQL (DocumentDB) API. Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella service exposing multiple APIs (Core/SQL (DocumentDB), MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). This Azure DocumentDB is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB — it's Microsoft's offering that evolved into Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct with nuance: the naming is confusing. The modern managed Mongo offering has been branded Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility / vCore). Historically 'DocumentDB' referred to the predecessor that became Cosmos DB. The open-source DocumentDB engine is also a separate project; the new product uses the open-source DocumentDB engine for vCore and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and the older Cosmos RU model.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB engine exposing the MongoDB wire protocol; it is not a stock mongod process. That means you should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect differences in behavior, limits, indexing and some unsupported commands. Applications must be tested against the target account and account-specific limits (partitioning, RU consumption, transaction scope).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB runs on the DocumentDB engine (open-source project) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol; standard drivers work, but platform-specific differences, limits and admin commands exist and must be validated.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (open-source engine note)

confusions.question: What database name will this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_banking_02 for all collections and operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the sample's run-environment explicitly directs using database name sample_banking_02.

grounding_links.title: Sample run-environment notes (skill_md) specifying sample_banking_02

confusions.question: Which Python client and ODM will the sample use to implement async Beanie-based ingestion?
confusions.cold_answer: Use motor (async MongoDB driver) as the Mongo client and Beanie ODM on top of motor/odmantic patterns (Beanie requires motor + pydantic). Installable via pip: pip install motor beanie pydantic.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Motor is the async driver; Beanie is the async ODM on top of Motor and Pydantic. Use Motor + Beanie for async ingestion in Python.
confusions.grounding_source: prompt prompt_review and documentdb-driver skill / learn docs showing driver compatibility

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (driver guidance)

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample use to summarise daily message volume and total value by message type?
confusions.cold_answer: An aggregation pipeline grouping by message_type and date (truncating timestamp to day) and summing count and amount. Example pipeline uses $dateTrunc + $group + $sum + $project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use an aggregation pipeline that date-truncates timestamps to the day and groups by day and message_type, summing amounts and counting documents; the $dateTrunc operator is available and the pipeline in the cold answer is appropriate.
confusions.grounding_source: prompt prompt_review and learn docs for aggregation operators

grounding_links.title: MongoDB aggregation (dateTrunc and group) compatibility docs and examples

confusions.question: Which environment variable and connection behavior will the sample use at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the Mongo connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime; ensure TLS and that the URI includes ssl=true (or use tls=True), correct port if not SRV.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: sample must read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment at runtime and not persist it; ensure TLS (tls=true or tls=True) and use the cluster-provided connection string, replacing placeholders for secrets at runtime.
confusions.grounding_source: prompt run-environment notes and connect docs

grounding_links.title: Development loop and connection best-practices (don't persist connection strings)

information_gaps.title: SWIFT MT103/MT202 canonical samples and field → schema mapping
information_gaps.description: No skill or documentation in the environment provides canonical sample MT103/MT202 raw messages or an authoritative mapping of SWIFT field tags (e.g., :20:, :23B:, :32A:, :50K:) to typed document fields the sample expects. I searched the installed documentdb-* skills and Microsoft Learn docs; these are about the DB service, not SWIFT message formats. The builder must provide example messages and a field mapping or the sample must assume a reasonable field set and document that assumption.

information_gaps.title: Exact package/version pins for Beanie + Motor + pymongo compatible with Mongo wire 7.0
information_gaps.description: The documentdb-driver skill and Microsoft docs say standard Mongo drivers work, but they don't list exact Python package versions guaranteed compatible with MongoDB wire 7.0 for Beanie + Motor + pymongo. The builder should pick and test specific versions (e.g., Motor & pymongo versions) against the live cluster; I searched the installed skills and Learn docs but found no pinned version guidance for Beanie+Motor targeting Mongo 7.0.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Do not treat Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb as the vCore-managed Mongo cluster resource — the correct resource type and CLI are Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and az documentdb mongocluster (see the mongoClusters ARM/Bicep docs).

sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the cluster-provided MongoDB URI (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and prefer the SRV form (mongodb+srv://...) where shown; for local dev use the DocumentDB local gateway image and its default port 10260 as documented (do not hardcode 10255/old suffixes).

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (SRV examples)
Development loop (DocumentDB local Docker gateway and port 10260)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Enable and use Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication if the sample or your environment requires role-based managed identities; enable authConfig.allowedModes on the cluster and follow the OIDC connection-string examples (MONGODB-OIDC) in the docs.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create vector indexes using the documented createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions 'kind' payload (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann) and parameters described in the vector-search docs rather than a generic MongoDB 'vector' createIndex call.

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds & parameters)

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH to make manual shell-based verification straightforward (install from MongoDB downloads or package manager). If installation is not possible, the sample README should document driver-based verification commands (python scripts that run the same checks) and show how to use the documentdb MCP tools to inspect data and indexes.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (mongosh examples)

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample; azd is only helpful for template-driven app deploys. Do not add unless the team wants azd-based CI/CD scaffolding.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful for provisioning the cluster via IaC, but the run-environment forbids creating a new cluster. Add only if you will include IaC templates that the builder will run later.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the sample run; include Terraform templates only if the sample repo wants to provide optional IaC artifacts. If provided, the agent kit should state how to apply them with az CLI / AzAPI providers when allowed.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python/Beanie sample.
